text: Abdul Bari (1892–1947) was an Indian freedom activist, academic, and social reformer who aimed to promote social reform in Indian society by educating people and awakening them to the need for change. He envisioned a free India free from slavery, social inequality, and communal disharmony and actively participated in the freedom movement, for which he was killed. He opposed the Two-nation theory. Born on 21 January 1884 to Md Qurban Ali as the eldest of four children, he was born in Kansua but resided in Koilwar and was a descendant of Malik Ibrahim Baya, a 14th-century sufi saint and warrior. He enrolled at the T. K. Ghosh Academy in Patna, completed his matriculation there, and later earned a Master of Arts degree from Patna University in 1918. In 1937, he signed his first historical agreement with the TISCO (now Tata Steel) management. He served as president of the Bihar Pradesh Congress Committee from 1946 until his death on 28 March 1947. He was killed by three men during an altercation at Bari Path in Khusrupur, Bihar Province, while returning from Dhanbad to Patna. Mahatma Gandhi described him as "living like a fakir in the service of his countrymen," while Congress President J. B. Kripalani called his death a loss of "India's bravest and most selfless soldier of freedom," emphasizing his complete absence of communal bias and his identity as an Indian dedicated to serving the working classes. On the first anniversary of his death, Rajendra Prasad remembered his contributions in a message dated 22 March 1948, published in Mazdur Avaz. Abdul Bari was married to Zulaikha Begum of Koilwar and had two sons—Salahuddin Bari and Shahabuddin Bari—and three daughters—Tahira, Hamida, and Saeeda. The Government of Bihar honored him by naming Bari Path and Abdul Bari Bridge. On March 20, 2021, and March 28, 2024, the Tata Workers Union, led by Sanjiv Kumar Chowdhary, president of the TWU, paid tribute to Abdul Bari on his death anniversary.
